pos: n. (a tomb, a burial place, especially one hewn in rock; rendering Hebrew qeber, Greek mnemeion, taphos)
etymology: From Latin sepulcrum, from sepelire, to bury. The KJV uses it for hewn rock tombs in particular — not a dug grave but a chamber, which is why a stone must be rolled to its door and why men can enter it and find it empty.
biblical_def: A sepulchre is a rock-hewn burial chamber, and the whole Christian faith turns on the emptiness of one of them. Matthew records the burial with deliberate legal precision: Joseph “laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock: and he rolled a great stone to the door of the sepulchre, and departed” (Matthew 27:60). Every detail closes a loophole — the tomb was new, so no other body lay in it; it was Joseph's own and identifiable; it was cut in rock, so there was no back way; and it was sealed with a stone and, in the next verses, a guard. Isaiah had specified the strange arrangement seven centuries earlier: “he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth” (Isaiah 53:9) — condemned as a criminal, buried as a rich man. The Lord Jesus also used sepulchres as His sharpest image for religious hypocrisy: “ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness” (Matthew 23:27). The whitewash was a public service, painted on tombs so pilgrims would not touch them and become unclean; the Pharisees had made themselves a warning sign. And He promised that these chambers will not hold: “the hour is coming, in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice” (John 5:28).
webster_summary: A rock-hewn burial chamber. Matthew documents the sealing of Christ's with legal care; Isaiah foretold a grave with the wicked and with the rich; Christ called hypocrites whited sepulchres and promised that all in the graves will hear His voice.
webster_full: SEPULCHER, SEPULCHRE, n. [L. sepulchrum, from sepelio, to bury.] A grave; a tomb; the place in which the dead body of a human being is interred, or a place destined for that purpose.
2. Among the Hebrews, sepulchers were often excavated in rocks, and closed with a great stone.
3. Whited sepulchers, an emblem of hypocrisy; fair without and foul within. Matt. 23.
SEPULCHRAL, a. Pertaining to burial, to the grave, or to monuments erected to the memory of the dead.
4. The Holy Sepulcher, the tomb in which the body of our Savior was laid.
scriptures: Matthew 27:60
And laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock: and he rolled a great stone to the door of the sepulchre, and departed.
Isaiah 53:9
And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.
Matthew 23:27
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness.
John 5:28
Marvel not at this: for the hour is coming, in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice,
corruption_summary: The empty sepulchre is downgraded from a fact about a location to a symbol of renewal — a spiritual resurrection in the disciples' hearts — which is precisely the resurrection Paul says would leave the whole faith vain.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberal theology since Schleiermacher and Bultmann has offered the church a resurrection without a vacated tomb: the Easter faith of the disciples, the persistence of Jesus' cause, the disciples' experience of forgiveness. Whatever else that is, it is not the apostolic claim. Paul stakes everything on a bodily event with witnesses who could be questioned, most of the five hundred still alive as he wrote (1 Corinthians 15:6), and states the consequence of the alternative without softening it: if Christ be not raised, our preaching is vain, your faith is vain, and we are found false witnesses of God (1 Corinthians 15:14-15). Matthew's pains over the new tomb, the great stone, the seal, and the watch make no sense as symbolism; they are the notes of a man establishing that a particular chamber was occupied on Friday and empty on Sunday.

There is a second corruption of the opposite temperament: the veneration of holy sepulchres. The Lord Jesus addressed it directly in the same chapter as the whited-sepulchre woe, charging the Pharisees with building the tombs of the prophets and garnishing the sepulchres of the righteous while being the children of those who killed them (Matthew 23:29-31). Tomb-building is an inexpensive way to honour dead prophets and avoid living ones. The relic-trade and pilgrimage economy that grew around holy sites was one of the abuses the Reformation named, and the reason is not aesthetic but doctrinal: the sepulchre's entire significance is that He is not there.
roots_summary: Hebrew qeber (grave, tomb) from qabar, to bury; Greek mnemeion (a memorial, hence a tomb) and taphos (a burial place, the word in Matthew 23:27).
roots_lines: Hebrew qeber (H6913) — a grave, sepulchre; the word in Isaiah 53:9 and throughout the patriarchal burial narratives.
Hebrew qabar (H6912) — to bury; the verb behind Machpelah, the first purchased sepulchre in Scripture (Genesis 23).
Greek mnemeion (G3419) — a memorial, tomb; from mnaomai, to remember; the usual resurrection-narrative word.
Greek taphos (G5028) — a burial place; the word in Matthew 23:27, 29 and Matthew 27:61, 64, 66.
Greek koniao (G2867) — to whitewash, plaster with lime; the participle rendered whited in Matthew 23:27.
usage: “His own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock” — every clause closes a loophole against the theft and swoon theories.
“Whited sepulchres… within full of dead men's bones” — the whitewash was a warning sign, and the Pharisees had become one.
“All that are in the graves shall hear his voice” — the sepulchre is a temporary arrangement.

pos: n. (a sacred tree or wooden image planted beside a pagan altar; rendering Hebrew asherah, eshel)
etymology: English grove, a small wood. The KJV translators used it for Hebrew asherah, which is properly the cult-object of the goddess Asherah — a wooden pole or carved image set up beside an altar rather than a stand of trees.
biblical_def: In the Authorized Version a grove is not scenery but an idol. The Hebrew word is asherah, the wooden cult-object of the Canaanite goddess of that name, planted beside an altar; and the law forbids it in the plainest terms: “Thou shalt not plant thee a grove of any trees near unto the altar of the LORD thy God” (Deuteronomy 16:21). The prohibition is not against trees but against syncretism — the grove goes near unto the altar of the LORD, which is exactly the problem. Israel did not usually abandon the LORD outright; she added. So Gideon's commission begins at home and at night, with a demolition: “throw down the altar of Baal that thy father hath, and cut down the grove that is by it” (Judges 6:25) — his father's altar, in his own yard, before he could deliver anyone else. Josiah's reformation is described in the same vocabulary of violence toward objects: “he brake in pieces the images, and cut down the groves, and filled their places with the bones of men” (2 Kings 23:14), defiling the sites so thoroughly that they could not be quietly reopened. The refrain that measures every king of Judah is whether the high places and groves came down; a reformation that leaves the groves standing is a change of policy rather than a change of worship.
webster_summary: Not a wood but an idol — the wooden cult-object of Asherah, set up beside an altar. The law forbids planting one near the LORD's altar; Gideon must cut down his own father's; Josiah destroys and defiles their sites.
webster_full: GROVE, n. [Sax. graf.] A cluster of trees, shaded by their foliage; a shady place.
2. In Scripture, a wood or cluster of trees consecrated to idolatrous worship, or the idol itself so planted. Deut. 16.
3. The heathen were accustomed to perform their idolatrous rites in groves, and hence the word came to denote the objects of that worship.
4. A walk covered by trees meeting above.
5. To plant with trees set in rows.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 16:21
Thou shalt not plant thee a grove of any trees near unto the altar of the LORD thy God, which thou shalt make thee.
Judges 6:25

And it came to pass the same night, that the LORD said unto him, Take thy father's young bullock, even the second bullock of seven years old, and throw down the altar of Baal that thy father hath, and cut down the grove that is by it:
2 Kings 23:14
And he brake in pieces the images, and cut down the groves, and filled their places with the bones of men.
Exodus 34:13
But ye shall destroy their altars, break their images, and cut down their groves:
corruption_summary: The commands to cut down groves are read as primitive intolerance, and the syncretism they address — adding another altar beside the LORD's rather than replacing it — is the exact form idolatry still takes.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern readers meet Deuteronomy 16:21 and Judges 6:25 with distaste: why must the trees come down, and why the vandalism? The answer is in the geography of the command. The grove is forbidden near unto the altar of the LORD; the offence is not that Canaanites worshipped Asherah in their own country but that Israel installed her equipment beside Yahweh's. That is syncretism, and it is the characteristic sin of the covenant people in every era — not the abandonment of God but the supplementing of Him. The first commandment does not say no other gods; it says no other gods before me, that is, in my presence, in addition. A God who tolerated the grove beside His altar would be a God indifferent to whether He is worshipped truly, which is the one thing Scripture never permits.

The contemporary groves are not carved. They are the additions a church makes beside the altar and calls enrichment: the therapeutic frame that supplies the real diagnosis while the gospel supplies the comfort; the political programme that supplies the real mission while worship supplies the motivation; the entertainment apparatus that supplies the real draw while preaching is kept as an ornament. In each case nothing is formally denied, and that is the mark of a grove. Gideon's pattern remains the model and remains costly: the demolition began with his own father's altar, at night, and the town wanted him dead by morning.
roots_summary: Hebrew asherah (H842), the wooden cult-object or the goddess herself; eshel (a tamarisk, rendered grove in Genesis 21:33); the Septuagint often renders asherah by alsos, a grove, which is where the English translation came from.
roots_lines: Hebrew asherah (H842) — the wooden image or pole of the Canaanite goddess; rendered grove throughout the KJV.
Hebrew eshel (H815) — a tamarisk tree; the word in Genesis 21:33 where Abraham plants a grove and calls on the LORD, a lawful planting.
Hebrew bamah (H1116) — a high place; the companion term, and the two are almost always destroyed together.
Greek alsos — a sacred grove; the Septuagint rendering that shaped the English translators' choice.
Hebrew massebah (H4676) — a standing pillar; the third member of the pagan triad of altar, pillar, and grove.
usage: “Near unto the altar of the LORD thy God” — the location is the offence; idolatry in Israel added rather than replaced.
“Cut down the grove that is by it” — Gideon's deliverance begins with his own father's altar.
“Filled their places with the bones of men” — Josiah defiles the sites so the worship cannot quietly resume.

pos: n. (a standing body of water, natural or built; rendering Hebrew berekah, agam, Greek kolymbethra)
etymology: Old English pol. In a land where water was scarce and cities were besieged, a pool was engineering rather than landscape — Hezekiah cut a tunnel to make one, and Jerusalem's survival depended on it.
biblical_def: A pool in Scripture is usually a built reservoir, and two of them frame the Gospel of John's theology of grace. The first is Bethesda: “there is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches” (John 5:2), where a multitude of impotent folk waited for a stirring of the water and a man had lain thirty-eight years without ever being first. The Lord Jesus heals him without the pool, without the stirring, and without his asking — a picture of sovereign mercy reaching the man who could never win the race. The second is Siloam, where a blind man is sent with clay on his eyes: “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.) He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing” (John 9:7). John pauses to translate the name because it is the point: the pool is Sent, and the One who sent him is Himself the Sent of the Father. Isaiah uses the image for the reversal of the curse in the wilderness — “I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water” (Isaiah 41:18) — and the historical books record the pools of Samaria, Gibeon, and Hebron as the fixed landmarks of a dry country, places where armies met and kings were killed.
webster_summary: A built reservoir in a dry land. At Bethesda a man who could never reach the water first is healed without it; at Siloam, the pool named Sent, a blind man washes and sees; Isaiah makes the wilderness a pool as the curse reverses.
webster_full: POOL, n. [Sax. pol.] A small collection of water in a hollow place, supplied by a spring, and discharging its surplus water by an outlet.
2. A body of standing water, without an outlet.
3. In Scripture, a reservoir constructed for the supply of a city; as the pool of Siloam, the pool of Bethesda, the upper pool.
4. In some countries, a small pond or lake.
5. The stakes played for in certain games.
scriptures: John 5:2
Now there is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches.
John 9:7
And said unto him, Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.) He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing.
Isaiah 41:18
I will open rivers in high places, and fountains in the midst of the valleys: I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water.
Isaiah 22:9
Ye have seen also the breaches of the city of David, that they are many: and ye gathered together the waters of the lower pool.
corruption_summary: Bethesda is preached as a lesson in perseverance — try harder and get to the water first — which reverses a narrative whose whole force is that the man never got there and was healed anyway.
corruption_paragraphs: The motivational reading of John 5 is remarkably durable: the man had an excuse ready, he blamed others, he should have found a way, and the sermon lands on personal initiative. Read the sequence. The Lord Jesus sees him, knows he has been long in that case, asks whether he will be made whole, receives an answer that is indeed a complaint rather than a request, and heals him regardless. The man does not know who healed him and cannot say afterward (v. 13). There is no faith recorded before the healing and no request. It is one of the plainest instances of unsought, unmerited, effectual mercy in the Gospels, and it is a poor exchange to trade it for a lesson in self-improvement. The pool with its stirring is the system that always favours the strongest, and Christ bypasses it entirely.

Siloam is corrupted in a different way, by treating the washing as the operative cause — a sacramental efficacy in the water, or a work the man performed to earn his sight. John forestalls both by translating the name. The pool is Sent, and the Gospel has been calling Christ the Sent One since chapter 3. The clay was made before the man moved, the command came from Christ, and the obedience was the means and not the merit. That distinction — obedience as instrument, never as ground — is the same one the Reformed confessions draw about faith itself, and this narrative teaches it in the concrete.
roots_summary: Hebrew berekah (a built pool or reservoir) and agam (a marshy or standing pool); Greek kolymbethra (a place for swimming or bathing, from kolymbao, to dive).
roots_lines: Hebrew berekah (H1295) — a pool, reservoir; used of the pools of Samaria, Gibeon, Hebron, and Siloam.
Hebrew agam (H98) — a marsh, standing pool; used in Isaiah 41:18 of the wilderness turned to water.
Hebrew shiloach (H7975) — Siloam, from shalach, to send; the softly-flowing waters of Isaiah 8:6.
Greek kolymbethra (G2861) — a pool for bathing; the word for both Bethesda and Siloam in John.
Greek apostello (G649) — to send forth; the verb behind John's translation of Siloam as Sent.
usage: “Whosoever then first after the troubling of the water stepped in” — the system that always favours the strongest, and which Christ bypasses.
“The pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent)” — John translates the name because the name is the point.
“I will make the wilderness a pool of water” — the reversal of the curse in the vocabulary of engineering.

pos: n. and v.i. (a source of water rising from the ground; to leap up or issue forth; rendering Hebrew mayan, maqor, Greek pege, hallomai)
etymology: Old English springan, to leap. The noun and verb are one word because a spring is water that leaps — and the Lord Jesus keeps the verbal force when He describes water “springing up into everlasting life.”
biblical_def: A spring is living water rising of itself, as opposed to a cistern which only holds what is poured in, and Scripture builds a whole doctrine on the difference. Jeremiah's indictment turns on it: Israel has committed two evils, forsaking the fountain of living waters and hewing out broken cisterns that can hold no water (Jeremiah 2:13). The Lord Jesus makes the promise correspondingly interior: “the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (John 4:14) — not a reservoir the believer must keep refilling but a source placed within him, which is the Spirit. Solomon uses the image for the moral consequences of a righteous man's collapse: “A righteous man falling down before the wicked is as a troubled fountain, and a corrupt spring” (Proverbs 25:26) — the damage is not private, because a fouled spring poisons everyone downstream, which is why the failure of a godly man is a public disaster. James applies the same physics to the tongue: “Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter?” (James 3:11). The question expects no, and the argument is that speech reveals a source. A man does not have a blessing-spring and a cursing-spring; he has one, and what comes out identifies it.
webster_summary: Water rising of itself, against the cistern which merely holds. Christ promises a spring placed within the believer; Solomon says a righteous man's fall fouls a public source; James argues that one fountain cannot yield sweet and bitter.
webster_full: SPRING, v.i. [Sax. springan.] To vegetate and rise out of the ground; to begin to appear; as, the corn springs.
2. To issue or proceed, as from a source; as, water springs from a fountain.
3. To leap; to bound; to jump.
SPRING, n. A leap; a bound; a jump.
6. A fountain of water; an issue of water from the earth, or the basin of water at the place of its issue.
scriptures: John 4:14
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.
Proverbs 25:26
A righteous man falling down before the wicked is as a troubled fountain, and a corrupt spring.
James 3:11
Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter?
Isaiah 41:18
I will open rivers in high places, and fountains in the midst of the valleys: I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water.
corruption_summary: John 4:14 is enlisted for a religion of inner resources — the divine spark, the true self, the wellspring within — when the entire clause depends on the water that I shall give him, a gift from outside that the man did not possess.
corruption_paragraphs: The line about a well springing up within is a favourite of every spirituality that locates salvation in the self: look inward, the answer is already there, drink from your own depths. The verse says the reverse in its own grammar. Twice in one sentence the Lord Jesus says the water that I shall give him; the spring is inside the man because Christ put it there, and before He put it there the woman had nothing but a bucket and a well that ran dry every day. This is precisely the Reformed doctrine of regeneration — a new principle of life implanted by the Spirit, not a latent capacity awakened. The interiority of the gift is real and glorious, and it is not native. Jeremiah 2:13 supplies the alternative on offer: a man who will not have the fountain does not thereby have nothing, he has cisterns of his own making, and they leak.

Proverbs 25:26 speaks to a second and more painful corruption, the modern instinct to treat a leader's fall as his own affair. Solomon calls the righteous man who gives way before the wicked a fouled spring, and the metaphor is chosen for its scope: a spring serves a town. When a man who has taught the truth abandons it under pressure, everyone who drank from him is affected, which is why Scripture holds teachers to a stricter judgment (James 3:1) and why the qualifications for elders are so heavily weighted toward character. The point is not that his sin is worse in kind; it is that his position makes it public water.
roots_summary: Hebrew mayan (a spring, fountain) and maqor (a source, wellspring — used of the heart in Proverbs 4:23); Greek pege (a spring or fountain) and hallomai (to leap, the verb in John 4:14).
roots_lines: Hebrew mayan (H4599) — a spring, fountain; used of literal springs and of the fountain of Israel in Psalm 68:26.
Hebrew maqor (H4726) — a source, wellspring; used in Proverbs 4:23 of the heart, out of which are the issues of life.
Hebrew mabbua (H4002) — a bubbling spring; the word in Isaiah 35:7 and 49:10.
Greek pege (G4077) — a spring, fountain; the noun in John 4:14 and James 3:11, and used of the fountain of the water of life in Revelation 21:6.
Greek hallomai (G242) — to leap, spring up; the vivid verb in John 4:14, elsewhere used of the lame man leaping in Acts 3:8.
usage: “The water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water” — interior, and given; never native.
“A troubled fountain, and a corrupt spring” — a righteous man's collapse fouls a public source.
“Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter?” — speech identifies the source it came from.

pos: n. (a blemish, stain, or moral fault; rendering Hebrew mum, tebullah, Greek spilos, amomos in the negative)
etymology: Middle English spotte, of Germanic origin. Its biblical career runs through the sacrificial law: the beast must be without spot, and the word then transfers to the Lamb and to the church He is preparing.
biblical_def: A spot is a blemish that disqualifies, and the word carries the entire sacrificial system into the New Testament. The law required animals without blemish; Peter identifies the fulfilment: redemption came “with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot” (1 Peter 1:19). Two terms are used, one for a defect of nature and one for a defect acquired — He was neither born flawed nor became stained, which is the sinlessness the atonement requires, since a spotted victim atones for nothing. Paul then makes the same word the goal of Christ's work on the church: He gave Himself for it, sanctifying and cleansing it, “that he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish” (Ephesians 5:27). The church is not spotless now — it is being made so, by a Husband who is Himself the one washing it. Moses uses the word in its harshest form to describe apostate Israel: “their spot is not the spot of his children: they are a perverse and crooked generation” (Deuteronomy 32:5), where even the blemish is of the wrong kind. And Jude describes false teachers as spots in the love feasts, feeding themselves without fear — the stain seated at the table.
webster_summary: A disqualifying blemish. Peter calls Christ a lamb without blemish and without spot; Paul makes a church without spot or wrinkle the goal of the cross; Moses says apostate Israel's spot is not the spot of God's children.
webster_full: SPOT, n. A mark on a substance made by foreign matter; a blot; a place discolored.
2. A stain on character or reputation; disgrace; reproach; fault; blemish. Deut. 32.
3. A small extent of space; a place; any particular place.
4. Without spot, without blemish; unblemished; as a lamb without spot. 1 Pet. 1.
SPOTLESS, a. Free from spot; free from impurity; pure; untainted; innocent.
scriptures: 1 Peter 1:19
But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot:
Ephesians 5:27
That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish.
Deuteronomy 32:5
They have corrupted themselves, their spot is not the spot of his children: they are a perverse and crooked generation.
James 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
corruption_summary: Ephesians 5:27 is used against the visible church — a demand for a pure congregation now, on pain of separation — which mistakes a promise about the church's presentation for a precondition of its legitimacy.
corruption_paragraphs: The spotless-church text has fuelled successive separatist movements: since Christ is preparing a church without spot, any congregation with visible spots must be abandoned for a purer one, and then that one abandoned in turn. Paul's grammar will not sustain the programme. Christ gave himself, that He might sanctify and cleanse, that he might present — a completed purchase, an ongoing washing, and a future presentation. The spotlessness is the destination, and the washing is being done by Christ through the word, in the churches as they are. The New Testament's own letters are addressed to congregations with incest, litigation, drunkenness at the table, and factions, and the apostolic remedy is discipline and teaching rather than departure. The dictionary holds the confessional position: churches are more or less pure, none is perfectly so this side of the presentation, and a purity that can only be maintained by continual separation ends in a church of one.

The opposite error takes the same verse as a licence for indifference — Christ will present her spotless, so present sanctification is optional. James answers it in a definition of religion the modern church rarely quotes whole: pure religion is visiting the fatherless and widows and keeping oneself unspotted from the world (James 1:27). The two halves are one sentence, and each is regularly used to excuse neglect of the other. Mercy without holiness and holiness without mercy are both spotted religion by James's reckoning.
roots_summary: Hebrew mum (a blemish disqualifying a sacrifice or a priest); Greek spilos (a stain, spot) and amomos (without blemish), with aspilos (unspotted) in James 1:27.
roots_lines: Hebrew mum (H3971) — a blemish, defect; the disqualifying mark on a sacrifice (Leviticus 22:20) or a priest (Leviticus 21:17).
Hebrew tamim (H8549) — complete, without blemish, perfect; the positive requirement for every offering.
Greek spilos (G4696) — a spot, stain; used in Ephesians 5:27 and of false teachers in 2 Peter 2:13.
Greek amomos (G299) — without blemish, faultless; used of Christ in Hebrews 9:14 and of the church in Ephesians 1:4 and 5:27.
Greek aspilos (G784) — unspotted, unstained; used in James 1:27, 1 Timothy 6:14, and 1 Peter 1:19.
usage: “A lamb without blemish and without spot” — neither flawed by nature nor stained by act; the sinlessness atonement requires.
“Not having spot, or wrinkle” — the church's presentation, worked by the Husband who washes her.
“To keep himself unspotted from the world” — half of James's definition of pure religion, and the half most often dropped.

pos: adj. (shared by all; also, ceremonially unclean, profane; rendering Greek koinos)
etymology: From Latin communis, shared. The Greek koinos holds both senses at once, and the collision of the two is the whole drama of Acts 10 — the same word means shared and defiled, because what is open to everyone is not set apart.
biblical_def: Common in the New Testament carries two senses that the book of Acts deliberately collides. In the ceremonial sense it means profane, not set apart, and therefore unfit — Peter's protest on the housetop uses it as a technical term: “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean” (Acts 10:14). The answer he receives abolishes the category by divine act rather than by argument: “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” (Acts 10:15), and the vision is repeated three times because Peter is about to walk into a Gentile house and needs to know that the barrier came down from heaven and not from his own liberality. In the other sense common means shared, and the same root describes the church's life: “all that believed were together, and had all things common” (Acts 2:44), and Paul greets Titus as his own son “after the common faith” (Titus 1:4), while Jude urges contending for the faith once delivered, having intended to write of the common salvation. The two senses are joined by the same Greek word koinos, from which comes koinonia, fellowship. What God has cleansed becomes shareable; the removal of the ceremonial barrier is exactly what creates the common life of Jew and Gentile in one body.
webster_summary: Both shared and profane, from one Greek root. Peter refuses what is common or unclean and is told not to call common what God has cleansed; the same word gives the church its common faith, common salvation, and all things common.
webster_full: COMMON, a. [L. communis.] Belonging equally to more than one, or to many indefinitely; as, life and sense are common to man and beast.
2. Belonging to the public; having no separate owner; as a common field.
3. Usual; ordinary; frequent.
4. Of no rank or superior excellence; ordinary; vulgar.
5. In Scripture, unclean; profane; not consecrated. Call not thou common. Acts 10.
scriptures: Acts 10:14
But Peter said, Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.
Acts 10:15
And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.
Acts 4:32
And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.
Titus 1:4
To Titus, mine own son after the common faith: Grace, mercy, and peace, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ our Saviour.
corruption_summary: Acts 10:15 has been lifted out of its dietary and Gentile-inclusion setting and made a general principle that no one may call anything unclean — a warrant for affirming whatever God has plainly called sin.
corruption_paragraphs: “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” is now regularly deployed as a proof-text for the affirmation of behaviours Scripture forbids: God has cleansed, who are you to call it unclean? The move ignores what the vision was about and what Peter himself said it was about. He interprets it in verse 28 — God has shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean — and the referent is Gentile persons, previously barred by ceremonial law from table fellowship. The abrogation is of the ceremonial code that separated Jew from Gentile, which the whole New Testament teaches was a temporary partition (Ephesians 2:14-15). It is not an abrogation of the moral law; the same apostles who received this vision wrote the epistles that name idolatry, fornication, and covetousness as excluding from the kingdom. God cleansed the meats and admitted the Gentiles; He did not repeal the seventh commandment.

The all things common of Acts 2:44 is corrupted in the parallel way, cited as a scriptural mandate for compulsory community of goods. Luke's own account resists it. The selling was voluntary and occasional, distribution followed need rather than equality, private ownership continued — Peter tells Ananias plainly that the land was his own and the money in his own power (Acts 5:4), so that his sin was lying and not withholding — and the practice belongs to a particular moment in Jerusalem. What the passage does establish, and what wealthy churches evade more often than they admit, is that a Christian's property is genuinely at his brother's disposal when there is need. That is a stiffer standard than most who cite the verse and most who dismiss it are living by.
roots_summary: Greek koinos (common, shared; hence ceremonially profane) and koinoo (to make common, defile); the same root yields koinonia, fellowship, and koinonos, a partner.
roots_lines: Greek koinos (G2839) — common, shared; in the ceremonial sense, unhallowed or defiled; the word in Acts 10:14, Acts 2:44, and Titus 1:4.
Greek koinoo (G2840) — to make common, to defile; the verb in Mark 7:15 and Acts 10:15 (call not thou common).
Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, communion, sharing; the same root, and the church's word for its shared life.
Greek akathartos (G169) — unclean, impure; the companion term paired with koinos in Acts 10:14.
Hebrew chol (H2455) — profane, common, not holy; the Old Testament counterpart, opposed to qodesh (holy) in Ezekiel 44:23.
usage: “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” — the ceremonial barrier removed by divine act, not human liberality.
“Had all things common” — voluntary, need-driven, and in a particular hour; property was still owned.
“After the common faith” — the one faith shared by Jew and Gentile, which the vision made possible.

pos: adj. (detestable to God; rendering Hebrew to'ebah and its cognates, Greek bdelyktos)
etymology: From Latin abominari, to deprecate as an ill omen. The Hebrew to'ebah is stronger and more personal: not a thing that offends taste but a thing God loathes, and Scripture applies it with a precision worth noticing.
biblical_def: Abominable renders a family of words meaning detestable to God, and the crucial point is what Scripture actually classes under it. Sexual sin is there: “Thou shalt not lie with mankind, as with womankind: it is abomination” (Leviticus 18:22). But so is a great deal that respectable religion never considers — false weights and unjust balances are an abomination (Proverbs 11:1); the proud in heart is an abomination (Proverbs 16:5); and most searchingly, worship itself becomes one when it is offered by a man who will not hear God's law: “He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination” (Proverbs 28:9). Solomon's catalogue of seven things the LORD hates puts a proud look first and him that soweth discord among brethren last (Proverbs 6:16-19), and neither is the sort of sin that gets a man removed from a congregation. Revelation places the abominable in the final list of the excluded, in company that includes both the expected and the unexpected: “the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars” (Revelation 21:8) — where the fearful head the list and all liars close it. The word is God's, not a term of social disapproval, and He assigns it.
webster_summary: Detestable to God. Scripture assigns the word to sexual sin, but also to false balances, a proud look, sowing discord, and the prayer of a man who will not hear the law; Revelation lists the fearful and all liars alongside the abominable.
webster_full: ABOMINABLE, a. [L. abominabilis.] Very hateful; detestable; loathsome.
2. Unclean; impure; in the ceremonial sense of the Mosaic law.
3. In Scripture, that which is detestable to God; as, the abominable thing which I hate. Jer. 44.
ABOMINATION, n. Extreme hatred; detestation.
4. The object of detestation, a common signification in Scripture; as, an idol is called an abomination.
scriptures: Leviticus 18:22
Thou shalt not lie with mankind, as with womankind: it is abomination.
Proverbs 28:9
He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination.
Revelation 21:8

But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.
Proverbs 11:1
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
corruption_summary: The word is handled selectively from both directions — wielded as a club on one sin while the commercial and relational abominations go unmentioned, or dismissed as tribal disgust-language that a mature reader may set aside entirely.
corruption_paragraphs: The revisionist argument runs that to'ebah marks ritual impurity or cultural distaste rather than moral evil, so that Leviticus 18:22 stands with shellfish and mixed fabrics as ceremonial law now expired. The text will not divide that way. Leviticus 18 is a chapter of sexual prohibitions — incest, adultery, child sacrifice to Molech, bestiality — and it grounds them not in Israel's ceremonial distinctness but in the conduct for which the Canaanites were being expelled, applying them to the stranger as well as the home-born. Ceremonial statutes were never charged against the nations. The New Testament repeats the moral judgment without the ceremonial apparatus in Romans 1:26-27 and 1 Corinthians 6:9-10, which settles the question for anyone who holds the whole canon. The dictionary states this plainly and states with it the pastoral distinction Scripture makes: every person is an image-bearer to be dealt with truthfully and kindly, and no sin named here is beyond the blood of Christ — Paul adds to that very list, and such were some of you.

The opposite corruption is committed by people who quote the verse loudest. If abomination is God's word, His other uses of it are equally binding, and they land closer to home: the false balance in Proverbs 11:1 indicts commercial dishonesty; Proverbs 6:16-19 puts a proud look, a lying tongue, and the sowing of discord among brethren in the same category; and Proverbs 28:9 declares the prayers of a man who will not hear the law to be abomination, which is a verdict on religious people specifically. A church that thunders about one abomination while tolerating the six that describe its own members has not taken the word seriously; it has taken it selectively, and Scripture calls that a divers weight.
roots_summary: Hebrew to'ebah (a detestable thing, abomination), sheqets (a detested unclean thing), and ta'ab (to abhor); Greek bdelygma (an abomination) and bdelyktos (abominable).
roots_lines: Hebrew to'ebah (H8441) — an abomination, detestable thing; used of idolatry, sexual sin, false weights, and the prayer of the disobedient.
Hebrew sheqets (H8263) — a detestable thing, especially of unclean creatures in the dietary law; a narrower and more ceremonial term.
Hebrew ta'ab (H8581) — to abhor, loathe; the verb from which to'ebah is formed.
Greek bdelygma (G946) — an abomination; the word in the abomination of desolation (Matthew 24:15) and in Revelation 21:27.
Greek bdelyktos (G947) — abominable; used in Titus 1:16 of those who profess to know God but in works deny Him.
usage: “A false balance is abomination to the LORD” — the word covers the ledger as well as the bed.
“Even his prayer shall be abomination” — worship offered by a man who refuses the law.
“The fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable” — a list that begins with cowardice and ends with lying.

pos: adj. (devoted to destruction, under a ban or curse; rendering Hebrew cherem, Greek anathema)
etymology: From Old English acursod, cursed. It renders two heavy words — Hebrew cherem, a thing devoted irrevocably to God and therefore to destruction, and Greek anathema, which is that same word carried into the New Testament.
biblical_def: Accursed translates the Hebrew cherem, the ban: a thing so devoted to God that it may not be turned to any private use and must be destroyed. Jericho is placed under it, and the warning is exact: “keep yourselves from the accursed thing, lest ye make yourselves accursed, when ye take of the accursed thing, and make the camp of Israel a curse” (Joshua 6:18). Achan takes a garment, silver, and gold; the whole army is defeated at Ai; and the ban proves contagious, which is the point of the word. The Greek anathema carries it into the New Testament, where Paul uses it twice in ways that are almost unbearable to set side by side. He pronounces it on any preacher of another gospel, himself and angels included: “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8). And he wishes it upon himself for his kinsmen's sake: “I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Romans 9:3). The same apostle who will not soften the curse on false teaching would take the curse himself if it could save Israel. Both are the same love, and the resolution of both is Galatians 3:13 — Christ was made a curse for us.
webster_summary: Devoted to destruction under a ban. Jericho's cherem proves contagious through Achan; Paul pronounces anathema on any preacher of another gospel, and in the same epistles wishes himself accursed for his kinsmen.
webster_full: ACCURSED, part. a. Doomed to destruction or misery. The city shall be accursed. Josh. 6.
2. Separated from the faithful; cast out of the church; excommunicated.
3. Worthy of the curse; detestable; execrable.
ANATHEMA, n. [Gr.] Excommunication with curses; a curse or denunciation by ecclesiastical authority.
4. In its original sense, a thing devoted or set apart, and hence irrevocably given up.
scriptures: Joshua 6:18
And ye, in any wise keep yourselves from the accursed thing, lest ye make yourselves accursed, when ye take of the accursed thing, and make the camp of Israel a curse, and trouble it.
Galatians 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Romans 9:3
For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh:
Galatians 3:13
Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree:
corruption_summary: Galatians 1:8 is used as a licence for anathematising every disagreement, while its actual scope — another gospel, a different way of being justified — is ignored; and in the opposite error the verse is dismissed as sub-Christian severity.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's anathema is specific, and the specificity is the safeguard. He is not cursing men who differ on church polity, eschatology, or the mode of baptism; he is cursing the preaching of another gospel, which in Galatians means adding a work to faith as the ground of justification. The Judaizers of Galatia affirmed Christ, the resurrection, and the Scriptures; their error was one added requirement, and Paul treats it as the destruction of the gospel because a Christ who saves partly does not save at all. That precision is exactly what disappears when the verse is used to settle secondary controversies. A church that anathematises everything anathematises nothing in the end, because the word loses its edge through overuse — which is what happened to it in medieval and later ecclesiastical practice.

The opposite reaction, common now, treats Galatians 1:8 as an embarrassment: a lapse in temper, or first-century polemic we have outgrown. But Paul says it twice, deliberately, in consecutive verses, and includes himself and an angel from heaven in the scope — which is not the mark of a man losing control but of a man foreclosing every escape. The doctrinal reason is Romans 9:3 read alongside it: this same apostle would be damned in Israel's place if it were possible. He curses false gospels precisely because he loves the people they destroy. And the whole matter resolves at Galatians 3:13, where the curse falls on Christ instead of on us — which is why tampering with that gospel is the one thing Paul will not permit.
roots_summary: Hebrew cherem (a thing devoted, banned, given over to destruction) from charam, to devote; Greek anathema (a thing set up or devoted, hence accursed), the Septuagint's rendering of cherem.
roots_lines: Hebrew cherem (H2764) — a devoted thing, a ban; the term governing Jericho in Joshua 6-7.
Hebrew charam (H2763) — to devote irrevocably, to destroy utterly; the verb behind the noun.
Greek anathema (G331) — a thing devoted to destruction, accursed; the word in Galatians 1:8-9, Romans 9:3, and 1 Corinthians 16:22.
Greek katara (G2671) — a curse; the word in Galatians 3:13, and epikataratos, cursed, in the quotation of Deuteronomy 21:23.
Greek anathema vs. anathema (G334, accented differently) — the same form also means a votive offering set up in a temple (Luke 21:5), preserving the original sense of a thing devoted.
usage: “Lest ye make yourselves accursed” — the ban is contagious, which is why Achan's theft defeated an army.
“Though we, or an angel from heaven… let him be accursed” — Paul forecloses every exception including himself.
“I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren” — the same man, the same love.

pos: adj. and n. (without reverence toward God, impious; rendering Hebrew rasha, beliyya'al, Greek asebes)
etymology: English formation from un- and godly. It renders Greek asebes — a, without, and sebomai, to reverence: the ungodly man is not chiefly an immoral man but an irreverent one, and the immorality follows.
biblical_def: The ungodly are those without reverence toward God, and the Psalter opens by defining the blessed man against them in a descending sequence: “Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful” (Psalm 1:1). Walking, standing, sitting — the progression from passing interest to settled residence is the psalm's warning, and it begins with taking counsel, which is to say with accepting the ungodly man's account of how the world works. Jude piles the root on itself four times in one verse to describe the coming judgment: “to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him” (Jude 1:15). Paul uses the same word to state the astonishing object of the atonement: “when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6), and again in the sentence that Luther found decisive — God justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5). This is the doctrine of justification in its most offensive form, and Paul chose the offensive word deliberately. God does not justify the improved, the sincere, or the promising; He justifies the ungodly, on the ground of a righteousness supplied to them and not produced by them.
webster_summary: Without reverence toward God. Psalm 1 traces the descent from walking in their counsel to sitting in the seat of the scornful; Jude hammers the root four times over the judgment; and Paul says Christ died for the ungodly and that God justifies the ungodly.
webster_full: UNGODLY, a. Wicked; impious; neglecting the fear and worship of God, or violating his commands.
2. Polluted by wickedness, or by violation of God's law.
3. In Scripture, the class opposed to the righteous; as the counsel of the ungodly. Ps. 1.
UNGODLINESS, n. Impiety; wickedness; neglect of God and his commands.
5. Contempt of the divine character and government.
scriptures: Psalm 1:1
Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.
Romans 5:6
For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.
Jude 1:15

To execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him.
1 Timothy 1:9

Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners, for unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers,
corruption_summary: Ungodly has been reduced to a synonym for morally coarse — a description of other people's vices — which loses the word's actual content (irreverence toward God) and blunts the point of the verse that says Christ died for exactly such men.
corruption_paragraphs: In common religious speech ungodly now means roughly disreputable, and it is applied outward: the ungodly are the coarse, the vulgar, the obviously immoral, over there. The Greek locates it elsewhere. Asebes is the failure to reverence, and a man may be scrupulously respectable and thoroughly asebes, which is why Paul lists the ungodly alongside the profane in 1 Timothy 1:9 and why the Pharisees, not the publicans, drew Christ's hardest words. Psalm 1 makes the danger a matter of counsel before it is a matter of conduct: what the ungodly offer first is not an invitation to vice but an explanation of life that leaves God out. That is available in perfectly polite forms, and it is generally where the walking begins.

The graver loss is what happens to Romans 4:5 and 5:6 when the word is softened. Paul says God justifieth the ungodly, and the sentence is scandalous by design — it is precisely what a righteous judge must not do (Proverbs 17:15), and Paul knows it, which is why Romans 3:26 labours to show how God can be just and the justifier. The medieval system could not tolerate the sentence and read justification as the making-righteous of a man being gradually improved; the Reformation recovered it as a declaration made about the ungodly on the ground of an alien righteousness imputed. Every softening of the word softens the doctrine. If the justified are the mildly-in-need-of-help rather than the ungodly, then grace is assistance and not resurrection.
roots_summary: Hebrew rasha (wicked, guilty) and beliyya'al (worthlessness); Greek asebes (irreverent, impious, from a + sebomai, to reverence) and asebeia (ungodliness).
roots_lines: Hebrew rasha (H7563) — wicked, guilty, condemned; the word in Psalm 1:1 rendered ungodly.
Hebrew beliyya'al (H1100) — worthlessness, ruin; rendered ungodly men in 2 Samuel 22:5 and Belial elsewhere.
Greek asebes (G765) — irreverent, impious, ungodly; the word in Romans 4:5, 5:6, and 1 Timothy 1:9.
Greek asebeia (G763) — ungodliness, impiety; the first thing named in the revelation of God's wrath in Romans 1:18.
Greek sebomai (G4576) — to revere, worship; the positive root the alpha-privative negates.
usage: “Walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly” — the descent begins with an account of life that leaves God out.
“Christ died for the ungodly” — the object of the atonement stated in its most offensive terms.
“All that are ungodly… ungodly deeds… ungodly committed… ungodly sinners” — Jude will not let the word be softened.

pos: adj. and v.t. (empty, without content; also, annulled or of no effect; rendering Hebrew bohu, parar, Greek kenoo, katargeo)
etymology: From Old French voide, empty, from Latin vacuus. English keeps two senses that Scripture also keeps apart — empty of content, as in Genesis 1:2, and legally annulled, as in a vow or a covenant made void.
biblical_def: Void means empty, and Scripture uses it at the beginning, the middle, and the end of its argument. At the beginning: “the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters” (Genesis 1:2) — the Hebrew pair tohu wa-bohu, unformed and unfilled, describing the raw material God then shapes and fills over six days, forming on days one to three and filling on days four to six. Jeremiah quotes the phrase back as a picture of judgment: “I beheld the earth, and, lo, it was without form, and void” (Jeremiah 4:23) — sin runs creation backwards. In the legal sense, a vow may be made void by a husband's word (Numbers 30:12), and men may make void the law of God, which draws the psalmist's cry: “It is time for thee, LORD, to work: for they have made void thy law” (Psalm 119:126). Paul uses the same category in his argument for grace: “if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect” (Romans 4:14) — law-keeping and promise cannot both be the ground, because each voids the other. And over against everything that can be voided stands God's word, which cannot: “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isaiah 55:11).
webster_summary: Empty, or annulled. The earth begins without form, and void and is formed and filled; sin runs that backwards in Jeremiah; men make void God's law; law-as-ground voids the promise; but God's word never returns void.
webster_full: VOID, a. [Fr. vuide; L. viduus.] Empty; vacant; not occupied with any visible matter; as a void space or place.
2. Empty; unfurnished; unsupplied; wanting.
3. Having no legal or binding force; null; not effectual to bind parties; as a void contract.
4. Free; clear; as a conscience void of offence. Acts 24.
VOID, v.t. To make or leave vacant; to quit; to leave. 5. To annul; to nullify; to make of no validity or effect.
scriptures: Genesis 1:2
And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.
Isaiah 55:11
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Psalm 119:126
It is time for thee, LORD, to work: for they have made void thy law.
Romans 4:14
For if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect:
corruption_summary: Genesis 1:2 is pressed into service for the gap theory — a ruined earlier creation between verses 1 and 2 — and Isaiah 55:11 is stretched into a general warrant that any words spoken in faith will accomplish what the speaker pleases.
corruption_paragraphs: The gap theory reads the earth was without form, and void as became void, inserting a fall of Satan and the destruction of a pre-Adamic world between the first two verses of the Bible. It was popularised by Chalmers and carried into wide currency by the Scofield notes, largely as a way of accommodating long geological ages. The Hebrew does not support it: the verb is the ordinary hayah with a waw-disjunctive, giving a circumstantial description of the earth as created rather than a subsequent catastrophe, and Exodus 20:11 states that in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, leaving no room for a prior creation destroyed. The dictionary's position is the plain reading: tohu wa-bohu describes raw material at the outset of the week, unformed and unfilled, which God then forms on days one to three and fills on days four to six — a structure the chapter's own symmetry makes obvious.

Isaiah 55:11 has been annexed by the word-of-faith teaching, in which the principle that words do not return void is transferred from God to the believer, so that confession becomes creative and a spoken claim is expected to produce its object. Every term of the verse forbids it: my word, out of my mouth, that which I please, whereto I sent it. The efficacy belongs to the Sender, and the immediate context is the free pardon offered to the wicked who forsakes his way (v. 7). The comfort of the verse for a preacher or a parent is enormous and quite different from the promise being sold: the word of God that you scatter is not yours to make effectual, and it will not come back empty, though you may not live to see what it did.
roots_summary: Hebrew bohu (emptiness, void), paired with tohu (formlessness); parar (to break, annul, make void); Greek kenoo (to empty) and katargeo (to render inoperative).
roots_lines: Hebrew bohu (H922) — emptiness, void; occurring only three times, always with tohu (Genesis 1:2; Isaiah 34:11; Jeremiah 4:23).
Hebrew tohu (H8414) — formlessness, confusion, waste; used in Isaiah 45:18, where God says He created the earth not in vain (tohu).
Hebrew parar (H6565) — to break, frustrate, make void; the verb in Psalm 119:126 and in the annulling of vows in Numbers 30.
Greek kenoo (G2758) — to empty, make void; used in Romans 4:14 and, most weightily, of Christ emptying Himself in Philippians 2:7.
Greek katargeo (G2673) — to render idle or inoperative, make of none effect; the companion verb in Romans 4:14.
usage: “Without form, and void” — unformed and unfilled, the raw material God shapes and fills across the week.
“They have made void thy law” — the psalmist's ground for asking God to act.
“It shall not return unto me void” — the efficacy belongs to the Sender, not the speaker.
